title: Population and Settlement
syllabus: WAEC Geography, Regional Geography of Nigeria: population; Part B: world population, settlement
NERDC-based schemes: Population of Nigeria; Population; Settlements; Settlement interactions; Town/Village
objectives: state Nigeria's population size and explain how it is measured;
describe and explain the distribution of population in Nigeria;
discuss the effects of rapid population growth and migration;
classify settlements by size, pattern and function, with Nigerian examples;
explain the problems of urbanisation and suggest solutions.
calculate population density and the dependency ratio, and explain the causes and problems of urbanisation;
intro: Nigeria has the largest population in Africa, and it is growing quickly. Where people live, why they live there and how settlements grow are central questions in human geography. This lesson connects population with the physical setting you have already studied and with the economic activities you will study next.

blocks.text: A **census** is an official count of all the people in a country at a particular time, together with information such as age, sex and occupation. In Nigeria censuses are conducted by the **National Population Commission (NPC)**.

items: The **1991 census** counted about 89 million people.
The **2006 census** counted **140,431,790** people — the most recent census.

Since then the population has been **estimated**: United Nations estimates put it at about 228 million in 2023, and World Bank figures are similar or higher. Treat all figures after 2006 as estimates.

blocks.text: Nigeria's population is **youthful**: a large share — over 40 per cent by UN estimates — is under 15 years old. More than half of Nigerians are now estimated to live in urban areas. Accurate censuses are difficult because of the country's size, poor access to some rural areas, and disputes because population figures affect political representation and the sharing of revenue.
Population in Nigeria is **unevenly distributed**. **Population density** is the number of people per square kilometre of land.

blocks.caption: Simplified pattern of densely and sparsely populated areas.
blocks.credit: Map data: Natural Earth (public domain). Areas generalised for learning.

items.title: Densely populated
items.text: The south-west (Lagos, Ibadan and the Yoruba cities), the south-east (around Onitsha, Owerri and Aba) and the Kano–Katsina–Zaria area in the north.

items.title: Sparsely populated
items.text: Much of the Middle Belt, the Chad Basin in the north-east, parts of the Niger Delta swamps and rugged highland areas.

items: **Physical factors**: fertile soils and reliable rainfall attract farmers; swamps, rugged relief and very dry areas discourage settlement; the presence of water supports towns; diseases such as those spread by the tsetse fly historically discouraged settlement in parts of the Middle Belt.
**Economic factors**: industries, ports, mining and trade attract people, for example Lagos, Port Harcourt and Kano.

**Historical and political factors**: old kingdoms and cities such as Kano, Ile-Ife and Benin became population centres; past slave raiding reduced population in parts of the Middle Belt; government decisions such as building Abuja created new centres.

blocks.text: Nigeria's population grows mainly through **natural increase**: births are much higher than deaths. High fertility, early marriage, the value placed on large families and improved health care contribute to rapid growth.

items.title: Possible advantages
items.text: A large labour force, a large home market for goods and services, and potential for innovation and economic growth if people are educated and employed.

items.title: Problems
items.text: Pressure on schools, hospitals, housing and jobs; a high dependency ratio; overcrowding in cities; pressure on land and forests.

blocks.text: **Migration** is the movement of people from one place to another to live or work. In Nigeria the most important type is **rural–urban migration**, as young people move to cities in search of jobs, education and better services (**pull factors**), leaving behind poverty, lack of amenities and limited farm work (**push factors**). Seasonal migration also occurs, for example when people from the north move south during the dry season.

The **dependency ratio** compares the number of people in the dependent age groups (under 15, and 65 and over) with the number of working age (15–64). Because so many Nigerians are young, the country has a high dependency ratio: each working adult supports many children.

A **settlement** is a place where people live and carry out their activities. Settlements are classified as **rural** (villages and hamlets, mostly engaged in farming, fishing or other primary activities) or **urban** (towns and cities, mostly engaged in manufacturing, trade and services).

items: **Nucleated**: houses clustered together, often around a market, water source or road junction; common in many parts of Yorubaland and the north for security and shared services.
**Dispersed**: houses scattered among farms; common in parts of the south-east and on large farmlands.
**Linear**: houses built along a road, river, railway or coast.

blocks.text: The **site** of a settlement is the land it is built on (for example a hilltop, river bank or island); its **situation** is its position in relation to the surrounding area (for example at a river crossing or on a major route). Lagos grew on an island and lagoon site with an excellent situation for a port.

sections.title: Functions of towns and urban problems

blocks.text: **Urbanisation** is the increase in the proportion of a country's population that lives in towns and cities. In Nigeria it is caused by rural–urban migration, natural increase within the towns, and the growth of large villages into towns. Lagos, Kano, Ibadan, Abuja and Port Harcourt are among the largest and fastest-growing urban areas.

Settlements interact through trade, migration, transport, communication and services. Larger towns provide services such as hospitals, universities and specialised markets for the villages around them, forming a **settlement hierarchy** from hamlets to cities.

items: **Urban problems**: housing shortages and slums (for example Makoko in Lagos), traffic congestion, unemployment, inadequate water and electricity, poor waste disposal and flooding.
**Possible solutions**: urban planning and housing schemes, better public transport, rural development to reduce migration, waste management and drainage improvement, and job creation.

definitions: An official count of the population of a country at a particular time.
The number of people living per square kilometre of land.
Births minus deaths in a population over a period.
The number of dependants (young and old) compared with the working-age population.
The movement of people from one place to another to live or work.
The increase in the proportion of a country's population living in towns and cities.
Site: the land a settlement is built on. Situation: its position relative to its surroundings.
Something that encourages people to leave a place, such as unemployment or a lack of amenities.
Something that attracts people to a place, such as jobs, schools or hospitals.

worked.title: Calculating population density
worked.problem: A local government area has a population of 360,000 and an area of 1,200 km². Calculate its population density.
steps: Always give the unit: people per square kilometre.

worked.title: Calculating a dependency ratio
worked.problem: A village has 4,400 people aged under 15, 300 aged 65 and over, and 5,300 aged 15–64. Calculate its dependency ratio.
steps: = **88.7**, so there are about 89 dependants for every 100 people of working age.
worked.note: Illustrative figures, not census data for a real village.

exam_tips: For distribution questions, describe the pattern first (where dense, where sparse, with named areas) before explaining factors.
Separate physical, economic and historical factors in your answer; examiners reward clear organisation.
State clearly that post-2006 population figures are estimates.

checks.q: When was Nigeria's most recent census and what population did it record?
Name two densely populated areas of Nigeria and give one reason for each.
checks.a: The south-west (trade, industry and Lagos's port) and the Kano area (fertile soils, long history of trade and city life). The south-east is also accepted (fertile land, long-settled farming communities).

checks.q: What is the difference between a settlement's site and its situation?
checks.a: Site is the land it is built on; situation is its position relative to the surrounding area, such as routes and rivers.

checks.q: Give two reasons why accurate censuses are difficult in Nigeria.
checks.a: The country is large and some rural areas are hard to reach; and population figures affect political representation and the sharing of revenue, which leads to disputes and possible inflation of figures.

checks.q: Distinguish between the site and the situation of a settlement.
checks.a: The site is the actual land on which the settlement is built (for example an island or hilltop). The situation is its position in relation to the surrounding area, such as on a major route or at a river crossing.

summary: Nigeria's last census (2006) counted 140,431,790 people; recent estimates exceed 220 million. The population is youthful and increasingly urban.
Dense areas: the south-west, the south-east and the Kano–Katsina–Zaria area. Sparse areas: much of the Middle Belt and the Chad Basin.
Distribution reflects physical, economic and historical factors; rapid growth brings both opportunities and pressures.
Settlements are rural or urban, with nucleated, dispersed or linear patterns, and towns have administrative, commercial, industrial and other functions.

structured.q: (a) Describe the distribution of population in Nigeria. (b) Explain three factors responsible for this distribution.
model: (a) Population is unevenly distributed. Dense concentrations occur in the south-west (Lagos, Ibadan and other Yoruba cities), the south-east (around Onitsha, Owerri and Aba) and the Kano–Katsina–Zaria area in the north. Sparse areas include much of the Middle Belt, the Chad Basin in the north-east, swampy parts of the Niger Delta and rugged highlands.

(b) 1. Fertile soils and adequate rainfall support dense farming populations, as in the south-east and around Kano. 2. Economic opportunities in industry, trade and ports attract people to cities such as Lagos and Port Harcourt. 3. Historical factors: old cities and kingdoms such as Kano and Ile-Ife became centres of population, while slave raiding and the tsetse fly reduced population in parts of the Middle Belt.
points: Up to 6 marks for (a), with named areas.
3 marks for each factor in (b), explained with an example.

structured.q: (a) What is rural–urban migration? (b) Explain two causes and two effects of rural–urban migration in Nigeria.
model: (a) The movement of people from villages to towns and cities to live and work.

(b) Causes: people are attracted by jobs, education and better amenities in cities (pull factors), and pushed by poverty and lack of services in rural areas (push factors). Effects: overcrowding, slums and unemployment in cities; loss of young labour and reduced farm output in rural areas.
points: (a) 2 marks; (b) 2 marks for each cause and effect.

structured.q: (a) What is rural–urban migration? (b) Give two push factors and two pull factors. (c) Describe two effects of rural–urban migration on Nigerian cities.
model: (a) Rural–urban migration is the movement of people from villages and rural areas to live and work in towns and cities.
(b) Push: poverty and low farm incomes; lack of amenities such as electricity, schools and hospitals. Pull: better job opportunities; better schools, hospitals and services in cities.

(c) 1. Overcrowding, housing shortages and the growth of slums such as Makoko in Lagos. 2. Unemployment and pressure on water, electricity, transport and waste services, causing traffic congestion and poor sanitation.
points: 1 mark for each push and pull factor (4 marks).
2 marks for each effect, described with an example (4 marks).
